To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the presence of a glycol fog in the open-path FT- IR beam will lead to an interference in the measurement of the concentration of a low-concentration release of diethyl ether, and (2) the interference may be overcome by including background spectra in which a glycol fog is present in the calibration set for PLS or by the use of TFA. (i) the presence of glycol fog in the infrared beam gives rise to an interference that can only be overcome by the use of a calibration set that includes spectra in which the fog is present, and (ii) the presence of large water droplets in the beam does not give rise to an interference, so that accurate results can be obtained without the use of a precalibration.

(i) PLS regression and TFA both allow the presence of low concentrations of diethyl ether to be recognized under the conditions of a glycol fog and (ii) both techniques allow the presence of diethyl ether in the presence of large water droplets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of open-path FT- IR spectroscopy to detect the presence of chemical warfare agents in the atmosphere.
the detection of low concentration releases of chemical agents from a distance of a few hundred meters.
the detection of chemical agents in open air by open-path FTIR.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the case of open-path FT-ICR spectroscopy, the presence of a glycol fog in the beam would lead to a reduction in the sensitivity for the detection of low concentrations of a chemical agent, but the presence of rain would not.

the PLS calibration method is only applicable to the measurement of low concentrations in the presence of a background interference such as a glycol fog if a set of calibration spectra in which the interference is present is used.

PLS regression can be used for quantitative analysis when a glycol or other fog is present in the beam if background spectra are included in the calibration data set; TFA will always allow the presence of the target compound to be recognized, even when no background spectra are available.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for open-path FT- IR detection of trace concentrations of chemical agents in fog or in rain, PLS is a viable technique provided that background spectra are included in the calibration, whereas TFA is a viable technique for detection in rain but not for detection in fog.
PLS is more robust than TFA, but only under the conditions that the calibration set contains background spectra that are representative of the interference that is to be present in the field.
, for open-path FT-IRS, the use of PLS regression requires that the background spectrum be representative of the actual conditions in which the target is being sought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of water droplets in the beam is not a significant problem for open-path FT-IRS analysis, but the presence of a glycol fog is a serious problem.

the detection of low-concentration chemical releases in the atmosphere can be achieved by FT-IR spectroscopic techniques under conditions of severe interference, but that the type of interference must be known beforehand in order for appropriate data processing to be used.

the presence of background interference does not preclude detection of a target species by open-path FTIR, provided that the interference is either known or can be estimated from a calibration set that includes spectra of the background interference.
